title.value: A summary of our rebuttal and a revision of our manuscript has been updated.

comment.value:
We extend our gratitude to all the reviewers for your invaluable comments and feedback. We have diligently prepared a thorough response to address all your questions and have updated the revised manuscript in accordance with your suggestions.

We are encouraged by the positive comments from reviewers, including that: this framework employs a clever two-stage design that combines iterative candidate selection with pre-trained observer model filtering [**B2qG**], this approach avoids the complex and time-consuming optimization processes, making the dataset distillation process more efficient, straightforward, and easier to deploy [**B2qG**], OD$^3$ achieves extremely high compression ratios (up to 99.75%) on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC while maintaining the accuracy of trained models, providing an efficient solution for saving computational and data resources when training object detectors, enables extremely fast dataset synthesis and significantly reduces the computational overhead of the distillation process, OD$^3$ achieves strong performance with clear speed advantages—dataset synthesis on COCO takes ~4.7 hours on a single GPU, significantly faster than optimization-based alternatives [**B2qG**, **AKz7**, **NPmv**], the SA-DCE component provides a practical way to retain contextual cues for small objects, offering a useful insight for dataset distillation in detection [**NPmv**].

We also thank the reviewers for constructive comments and suggestions, such as clarifying the second contribution in the introduction that extends the concept of dataset distillation, Tables 1 and 2 should include upper bounds [**B2qG**], clarifying the screening module that removes objects deemed low-confidence by the observer model [**AKz7**], clarifying that the synthesis relies on instance copy-pasting, leading to a domain gap [**NPmv**]. We have accommodated all of the comments in our revised manuscripts, where all the revised contents are highlighted in $\textcolor{blue}{\text{blue}}$ color.

Detailed responses to each reviewer's questions, concerns, and requested changes are provided in the following replies. We are eager for you to review and explore our detailed responses. Although we understand that no further reviewer questions can be raised, we always welcome any additional discussion, and your insights are crucial to refining our paper.

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback. We have uploaded a revised version of our paper that incorporates all concrete revisions based on your suggestions. Below, we further provide detailed responses to address your concerns.

>W1: The second contribution in the introduction extends the concept of dataset distillation from the relatively well-explored domain of image classification to the more challenging task of object detection. This has already been achieved by DCOD.

Thanks for pointing this out. We agree that DCOD has previously demonstrated dataset distillation for object detection. We have clarified the contributions in our revised version to avoid implying that OD$^3$ is the first to extend distillation beyond image classification. Our contribution is instead centered on a training-free formulation that does not rely on iterative optimization with higher accuracy, which distinguishes OD$^3$ from DCOD. This change is reflected in lines 99-103.

>W2: Both DCOD and OD3 experience substantial performance degradation compared to their uncompressed counterparts. At compression rates of 5% or even 10%, it remains unclear how much additional compression would be necessary to approach the performance of the uncompressed models.

We appreciate the reviewer's comment. The table below summarizes the results for OD$^3$ under the suggested compression budgets. At 5.0% IPD, more than 75% of the full-scale performance is preserved. It is worth noting that DCOD has not reported results on those compression rates, and its code is not publicly available to generate those results and facilitate comparison. This table has also been added to the revised manuscript (lines 432-440). We also clarify that the performance degradation at extreme compression rates (e.g., 5%) is expected due to the inherent trade-off between limited data size and information capacity. Both DCOD and our work focus on exploring this extreme regime to push the boundary of efficient detection training, also enabling training in highly resource-constrained environments where uncompressed data is impractical. While our method outperforms prior SOTA by a large margin, and maintains usable detection accuracy.

| **IPD** | **mAP** | **mAP@50** | **mAP@75** | **mAP$_s$** | **mAP$_m$** | **mAP$_l$** |
|------|:-------:|:------:|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|:-----:|
|       5.0%      |       30.10      |    49.70     |     31.80    |      16.20     |    34.90   |  38.40   |
|       10.0%    |       31.80      |    51.70     |   34.10      |      16.80     |    36.70   |  40.50   |
|       20.0%    |       32.60      |    53.00     |   34.80      |      18.00     |    37.50   |  41.60   |
| 100% (Uncompressed Dataset)    |       39.80      |   60.60     |   43.50      |      22.40     |    43.90   |  51.90   |

>Q1: Tables 1 and 2 should include upper bounds to illustrate the potential for improvement in existing methods within the field of DD for object detection.

As suggested by the reviewer, we have reported the upper bounds of training on the whole dataset in Tables 1 and 2, which can be seen in lines 324-347 of the revised manuscript.

>Q2: Table 4 indicates that the best results are obtained when the observer and target detectors share the same architecture. Employing higher-performance detectors does not enhance the distillation effect. Therefore, it would be insightful to compare the performance of student models that also adopt DETR or other transformer-based architectures—that is, models of similar design.

Thanks for raising this point. We ran additional experiments using transformer-based detectors to investigate whether architectural matching with a DETR student would improve distillation. The results for 0.5% IPD are shown below:

| **Observer** | **Target** | **mAP** | **mAP@50** | **mAP@75** | 
|----|:-----:|:------:|:-------:|:-------:|
|       Faster R-CNN    |       Deformable DETR      |    6.00     |     12.20    |      5.50    |  
|       Deformable DETR |       Deformable DETR      |    9.40     |   18.80      |      8.60    | 
|       Faster R-CNN    |       Faster R-CNN         |    17.20    |   39.50      |      22.90   | 

These experiments highlight a consistent pattern: transformer-based detectors are more data-hungry compared to CNN-based ones [1]. DETR and its variants are known to require large datasets, long optimization schedules, and abundant object diversity to converge well. When the distilled dataset is extremely small, these models struggle to learn effective queries and attention patterns. In contrast, Faster RCNN performs markedly better under severe data scarcity. Its inductive biases (region proposals, convolutional hierarchies, and structured box regression) allow it to generalize efficiently from limited data.

--------------
References:

[1] Wang, Wen, et al. "Towards data-efficient detection transformers." European conference on computer vision. Springer Nature Switzerland, 2022.

summary.value: OD3 is an optimization-free dataset distillation framework for object detection that synthesizes compact datasets by iteratively placing and screening object instances using a pre-trained observer model. It achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing prior methods by over 14% in mAP50 on COCO at 1% compression ratio.

strengths.value:
1.OD3 achieves strong performance with clear speed advantages—dataset synthesis on COCO takes ~4.7 hours on a single GPU, significantly faster than optimization-based alternatives.

2.The SA-DCE component provides a practical way to retain contextual cues for small objects, offering a useful insight for dataset distillation in detection.

weaknesses.value:
1. The synthesis relies on instance copy-pasting, leading to a domain gap between synthetic and real images that may limit generalization.

2. The method depends on a pre-trained observer model; if this model is biased (e.g., performs poorly on certain categories), it may filter out valid instances and introduce distillation bias.

3. Performance at higher compression ratios (e.g., 5%，10%，20%，100%) is not explored, leaving the scalability and upper performance bound unclear.

4. Backgrounds are randomly sampled from the original dataset, which can create semantically implausible scenes (e.g., indoor objects placed on outdoor backgrounds).

comment.value:
Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback. We have carefully revised our manuscript based on your suggestions and uploaded an updated version accordingly. Below, we provide detailed point-by-point responses addressing each of your comments.

>W1: The screening module directly removes objects deemed low-confidence by the observer model. However, these low-confidence objects could precisely be the "hard examples"—such as rare categories, heavily occluded, or unusually shaped objects—that are crucial for training a robust detector.

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment. Although OD$^3$ removes detections with observer confidence below 0.2, this threshold is intentionally conservative and serves only to eliminate unreliable proposals, rather than challenging or informative instances. This threshold was empirically proven to give the best performance, as shown in Table 8 in the appendix. We also highlight that OD$^3$ includes a dedicated mechanism specifically designed to preserve hard examples, particularly small or context-poor objects. The proposed Scale-Aware Dynamic Context Extension (SA-DCE) mechanism expands each object's bounding region adaptively based on its size, ensuring that small and easily occluded objects retain sufficient semantic and spatial context. This prevents the observer from misclassifying such instances as low-confidence and filtering them out. In addition, we include visualizations of a sample of objects removed by the observer model in Figure 9 of the revised manuscript (Appendix). These filtered-out low-confidence regions predominantly correspond to background areas, nonsensical patterns, or unrecognizable pixel signals, and can effectively be regarded as "visual noise".

>W2: The final optimization objective does not account for inter-class balance and intra-class diversity, both of which are critical for the object detection task. The current metrics for Information Density (Φ) and Diversity (N) are too coarse and may lead to a distilled dataset that is biased towards dominant or easy-to-detect classes.

We appreciate the reviewer's careful observation. Our method addresses inter-class balance and intra-class diversity through the segment-based synthesis strategy described in Section 3.1 and visualized in Figure 3. Formally, we divide the training set into non-overlapping segments $\mathcal{T}^1, \mathcal{T}^2, \dots, \mathcal{T}^K$ ($K=IPD$), where each segment $\mathcal{T}^k$ corresponds to a subset of the full dataset with controlled class distributions and internal diversity. For each distilled image ${\bf{x}}_i$, we randomly select source objects from the corresponding $\mathcal{T}^k$, enforcing: 1) Each $\mathcal{T}^k$ is constructed to represent a class-balanced subset. 2) Sampling within $\mathcal{T}^k$ avoids overlapping from the same original images and objects across the distilled images to preserve diversity.

To further assess whether OD$^3$ introduces inter-class bias, we compared per-class mAP50 between the baseline model (trained on the full dataset) and the OD$^3$ model (trained on only 0.5% and 1% of the data) on MS COCO. The Spearman rank correlation is as follows:

| IPD | Spearman rank correlation | p-value |
|-----------|:---------:|:-------------:|
|       0.5%  |      0.862    |   7.8×10$^{-25}$  |   
|       1.0%  |      0.903    |   2.6×10$^{-30}$  | 


This indicates a strong and statistically significant preservation of class-level performance patterns. In addition to the per-class performance analysis, we examined the distribution of semantic supercategories in the synthesized datasets. As shown in Fig. 8 of the appendix, the probability distribution of supercategories in the 0.25%, 0.5%, and 1.0% synthetic sets closely matches that of the original MS COCO dataset, indicating that the synthesis procedure preserves the underlying class structure and does not skew the dataset toward specific groups.

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments. We have carefully revised our paper and uploaded an updated version that incorporates concrete changes based on your suggestions. Below, we provide a detailed response addressing each of your feedback and concerns.

>W1: The synthesis relies on instance copy-pasting, leading to a domain gap between synthetic and real images that may limit generalization.

Thanks for pointing this out. We clarify that our instance-level synthesis is designed to preserve visual realism by copying objects directly from real images without artificial rendering or generation. Our focus, consistent with almost all prior works in dataset distillation, is on the absolute downstream task performance. Most prior reputable methods (e.g., [1-3]) either compromise spatial structure by stacking multiple objects into a single image (e.g., RDED), or generate images that significantly deviate from the original ones (e.g., DCOD and SRe$^2$L), yet still achieve strong downstream performance. Realism is neither a prerequisite nor a stated goal in this research line. Our results show that high task performance can be achieved without enforcing strict global visual realism.

>W2: The method depends on a pre-trained observer model; if this model is biased (e.g., performs poorly on certain categories), it may filter out valid instances and introduce distillation bias.

We appreciate the reviewer's careful observation. We clarify that our observer filtering is not based on hard filtering but on soft scores, allowing instances from underrepresented categories to still be retained with lower weight. Actually, the reliance on a pre-trained observer is indeed a general characteristic of all distillation pipelines. To examine whether observer bias has a meaningful impact on the distilled data, we explicitly evaluated cross-architecture generalization as shown in Table 4. The distilled datasets transfer robustly across heterogeneous detector families: two-stage (Faster R-CNN), one-stage (RetinaNet), and transformer-based detectors (ViTDet, Deformable DETR). These empirical results demonstrate robust performance across categories, showing limited impact from any potential observer bias.

>W3: Performance at higher compression ratios (e.g., 5%，10%，20%，100%) is not explored, leaving the scalability and upper performance bound unclear.

We appreciate the reviewer's comment. The table below summarizes the results for OD$^3$ under the suggested compression budgets. At 5.0% IPD, more than 75% of the full-scale performance is preserved. As more synthesized data are allocated (5\%–20\% IPD), performance rises steadily across all COCO metrics, indicating that our OD$^3$ scales in a predictable and stable manner. It is worth noting that DCOD has not reported results on those compression rates and its code is not publicly available to generate those results and facilitate comparison. This table has also been added to the revised manuscript (lines 432 to 440).

| **IPD** | **mAP** | **mAP@50** | **mAP@75** | **mAPs** | **mAPm** | **mAPl** |
|---|:--:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:----:|:--:|
|       5.0%      |       30.10      |    49.70     |     31.80    |      16.20     |    34.90   |  38.40   |
|       10.0%    |       31.80      |    51.70     |   34.10      |      16.80     |    36.70   |  40.50   |
|       20.0%    |       32.60      |    53.00     |   34.80      |      18.00     |    37.50   |  41.60   |
| 100% (Uncompressed Dataset)    |       39.80      |   60.60     |   43.50      |      22.40     |    43.90   |  51.90   |

>W4: Backgrounds are randomly sampled from the original dataset, which can create semantically implausible scenes (e.g., indoor objects placed on outdoor backgrounds).

Thanks for pointing this out. We clarify that while backgrounds are sampled from the original dataset, we ensure maintaining category consistency by only selecting backgrounds from scenes that share similar semantic contexts (randomly sampling backgrounds from the dominant COCO supercategory in the constructed image). Furthermore, we find that this diversity in background placement acts as a potential regularizer and actually enhances the model's robustness, rather than impairing learning. Our empirical results in Tables 1 and 2 show that the distilled detectors maintain high performance even when trained with such variations, suggesting that the model learns to focus on foreground-relevant features rather than overfitting to spurious background cues.

---------------

References:

[1] Qi, Ding, et al. "Fetch and forge: Efficient dataset condensation for object detection." In NeurIPS 2024.

[2] Sun, Peng, et al. "On the diversity and realism of distilled dataset: An efficient dataset distillation paradigm." In CVPR 2024.

[3] Yin, Zeyuan, et al. "Squeeze, recover and relabel: Dataset condensation at imagenet scale from a new perspective." In NeurIPS 2023.

Thank you for your response. All my questions have been resolved. I have one final suggestion: consider moving the reply to Q2 to the appendix. Additionally, Transformer-based methods tend to struggle when trained with limited synthetic samples, which may represent a valuable direction for future exploration in the DD field.

>W3: The core of the method involves placing objects randomly on a canvas with only an overlap ratio as a constraint. This ignores the spatial layout relationships, relative scales, and co-occurrence contexts of objects in the real world. Consequently, the synthesized images may lack semantic realism, which could limit the detector's ability to learn high-level contextual reasoning.

Thanks for the comment. We clarify that despite the absence of explicit modeling of spatial or contextual relationships, our distilled datasets yield strong performance across multiple detectors and real-world benchmarks, suggesting that modern object detectors can effectively learn high-level understanding even from such simplified compositions. This is also consistent with almost all prior works in dataset distillation. Similar to the prior methods, our focus is on the absolute downstream task performance. Most prior reputable methods (e.g. [1-3]) produce images that deviate from natural appearance but still deliver strong accuracy gains; realism is neither a prerequisite nor a stated goal in this research line. Our results show that high task performance can be achieved without enforcing strict visual realism.

--------------

References:

[1] Qi, Ding, et al. "Fetch and forge: Efficient dataset condensation for object detection." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 119283-119300.

[2] Cazenavette, George, et al. "Dataset distillation by matching training trajectories." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

[3] Yin, Zeyuan, Eric Xing, and Zhiqiang Shen. "Squeeze, recover and relabel: Dataset condensation at imagenet scale from a new perspective." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2023): 73582-73603.
Thanks for the follow-up suggestion. We have moved the reply to Q2 to the appendix of the revised manuscript as recommended (lines 864-877).

summary.value: This paper introduces $\text{OD}^3$ (Optimization-free Dataset Distillation for Detection), a novel framework explicitly designed to address the unique challenge of synthesizing small, high-fidelity datasets for object detection, a task more complex than image classification due to its spatial and semantic demands. $\text{OD}^3$ leverages a training-free, two-stage process—candidate selection followed by screening using a pre-trained "observer" model—to strategically reconstruct diverse, labeled training images without complex optimization. Evaluations on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC demonstrate that $\text{OD}^3$ effectively achieves significant dataset size reduction (up to $99.75\%$) while successfully maintaining the accuracy of object detection models.

strengths.value:
1. This framework employs a clever two-stage design that combines iterative candidate selection with pre-trained observer model filtering. This approach avoids the complex and time-consuming optimization processes typical of traditional DD methods, making the dataset distillation process more efficient, straightforward, and easier to deploy.

2. $\text{OD}^3$ achieves extremely high compression ratios (up to 99.75%) on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC while maintaining the accuracy of trained models, providing an efficient solution for saving computational and data resources when training object detectors.

weaknesses.value:
1. The second contribution in the introduction extends the concept of dataset distillation from the relatively well-explored domain of image classification to the more challenging task of object detection. This has already been achieved by DCOD.
2. Both DCOD and OD3 experience substantial performance degradation compared to their uncompressed counterparts. At compression rates of 5% or even 10%, it remains unclear how much additional compression would be necessary to approach the performance of the uncompressed models.

questions.value:
1. Tables 1 and 2 should include upper bounds to illustrate the potential for improvement in existing methods within the field of DD for object detection.
2. Table 4 indicates that the best results are obtained when the observer and target detectors share the same architecture. Employing higher-performance detectors does not enhance the distillation effect. Therefore, it would be insightful to compare the performance of student models that also adopt DETR or other transformer-based architectures—that is, models of similar design.

summary.value:
This paper introduces OD³, a novel, optimization-free framework for dataset distillation specifically designed for object detection. The method uses a two-stage process of candidate selection and screening to create small, efficient datasets. The work was reviewed by three experts in the field, who unanimously acknowledged the novelty and efficiency of the proposed method, leading to a consistent set of scores: **[6, 6, 6]**.

The initial reviews raised several valid concerns regarding the experimental validation, potential biases, and methodological choices. However, the authors provided an **exemplary and comprehensive rebuttal**, addressing every single point with additional experiments, detailed analysis, and manuscript revisions. This productive discussion phase, particularly the explicit confirmation from one reviewer that all their concerns were resolved, solidified the paper's standing.

The paper presents a valuable and well-executed contribution to the field of dataset distillation. The authors' thorough and convincing rebuttal successfully addressed all major reviewer concerns, transforming a potentially borderline paper into a solid accept.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The authors successfully addressed every major concern raised by the reviewers.

**Addressed Concerns:**   

   *  **Experimental Completeness:** The authors provided a new table with results at 5%, 10%, and 20% compression ratios and added the upper-bound performance to all relevant tables in the revised manuscript. This fully addressed the concern.

   *   **Hard Examples & Observer Bias:** The authors clarified that the filtering threshold is conservative. More importantly, they highlighted the **SA-DCE** mechanism designed to preserve small objects and provided visualizations showing that filtered-out instances were mostly noise. They also demonstrated strong cross-architecture generalization, mitigating fears of observer bias.

   *   **Lack of Realism:** The authors convincingly argued that achieving visual realism is not the goal of dataset distillation, a stance consistent with prior state-of-the-art work in the field. They proved that high task performance can be achieved without it.

   *   **Fairness and Diversity:** The authors explained their segment-based synthesis strategy, which enforces class-balanced subsets. They backed this up with a new analysis showing a high Spearman correlation for per-class performance and a supercategory distribution that closely matched the original COCO dataset.

   *   **Architectural Generalization:** The authors conducted new experiments with Transformer-based detectors (DETR), showing that these models struggle with the small distilled datasets, and provided a sound explanation related to their data-hungry nature, thereby fully answering the reviewer's question.


Reviewer B2qG explicitly stated, **"All my questions have been resolved."** The other two reviewers did not raise further issues after the rebuttal, and their scores remained at a level of acceptance. Therefore, there are no outstanding concerns.

reviewer_scores.value:
In this case, all reviewers participated in the rebuttal, and one (B2qG) participated in a follow-up discussion. The scores of all three reviewers remained unchanged at **6** after the rebuttal. This stability should be interpreted as a **confirmation of their initial positive assessment**.

The authors' comprehensive rebuttal eliminated the risk and confirmed the paper's quality. By resolving all major concerns, the authors solidified the score of 6, transforming it from a tentative, high-risk "marginal accept" to a confident, low-risk "solid accept." Had the rebuttal been weak, the scores would have likely dropped to 4.

summary.value: This paper proposes OD³, an optimization-free framework for dataset distillation in object detection. The method synthesizes a compact dataset by strategically selecting and placing object instances from the original dataset onto blank canvases and then screening them using a pre-trained observer model.

strengths.value: The proposed "optimization-free" paradigm, which employs a rule-based placement and screening strategy, enables extremely fast dataset synthesis and significantly reduces the computational overhead of the distillation process itself.

weaknesses.value:
1. The screening module directly removes objects deemed low-confidence by the observer model. However, these low-confidence objects could precisely be the "hard examples"—such as rare categories, heavily occluded, or unusually shaped objects—that are crucial for training a robust detector.
﻿
2. The final optimization objective does not account for inter-class balance and intra-class diversity, both of which are critical for the object detection task. The current metrics for Information Density (Φ) and Diversity (N) are too coarse and may lead to a distilled dataset that is biased towards dominant or easy-to-detect classes.

﻿3.  The core of the method involves placing objects randomly on a canvas with only an overlap ratio as a constraint. This ignores the spatial layout relationships, relative scales, and co-occurrence contexts of objects in the real world. Consequently, the synthesized images may lack semantic realism, which could limit the detector's ability to learn high-level contextual reasoning.
